blocks.html:
This section runs one regression analysis from question to report, in the order a Community Medicine researcher would, using only tools built in this chapter.

Research question. Among children aged 12 to 36 months attending a district under-five clinic, is household wealth associated with weight (kg), independent of the child’s age and sex?

Study design. A cross-sectional survey of 240 children attending the clinic over three months, with weight, age, sex and a household wealth index recorded at a single visit (data/journey_mlr.csv).

Outcome. Weight in kilograms: continuous, so linear regression is the natural first choice. (An alternative outcome is the weight-for-age z-score, recall §5.7.2.2.3, which is already standardised for age and sex; age would then not be entered as a covariate. This analysis keeps raw kilograms and adjusts for age and sex directly.)

Predictors and why each is there. Wealth index (continuous) is the exposure. Age in months enters for two separate reasons. First, it is a strong determinant of weight (r = 0.61 in these data), so including it removes a large part of the residual variation and makes the wealth coefficient more precise: a precision covariate. Second, age is a potential confounder: it cannot be caused by household wealth, and it would distort the crude wealth–weight comparison if wealthier and poorer households brought children of different ages to the clinic. That second condition was judged plausible before the analysis (care-seeking patterns differ by wealth); in this sample age and wealth correlate at r = 0.16. Sex is a determinant of weight with no plausible link to household wealth, so it enters as a precision covariate only.

Data preparation. Sex is coded 0/1 with boys as reference (§12.4.3). Three children (1.25%) have a missing wealth index. There is no evident reason why wealth data were missed differently for any group, so the analysis uses the 237 complete cases and says so; a larger or patterned loss would need the missing-data methods of §15.4 (such as multiple imputation).

Crude analysis. Weight on wealth alone: 0.90 kg per wealth-index unit (95% CI 0.52 to 1.29).

Model specification. Weight is regressed on wealth, age and sex together. The predictors were chosen by the subject-matter reasoning above, not by an automated search.

Assumptions. Linearity: residuals against fitted values show no curve, and a spline for wealth adds nothing (§12.4.5). Normality and equal variance: the Q-Q and Scale-Location plots look acceptable. Independence: each child attended once and no household contributed two children.

Diagnostics. Multicollinearity is negligible: every VIF is 1.03 or less (§12.4.4.1). One child, J090 (33 months, girl, wealth index −0.20, 17.6 kg), has a standardised residual of 3.73: a very heavy child from a below-average-wealth household. Her Cook’s D is 0.077, the largest in the data. Nothing suggests a data-entry error, so she is retained. Refitting without her moves the wealth coefficient from 0.62 to 0.65 kg: the conclusion does not depend on her.

m  <- read.csv("data/journey_mlr.csv")
m$sex <- factor(m$sex, levels = c("M", "F"))
cc <- na.omit(m)                          # 237 complete cases
crude <- lm(weight_kg ~ wealth_index, data = cc)
fm    <- lm(weight_kg ~ wealth_index + age_months + sex, data = cc)
round(cbind(coef(crude), confint(crude)), 2)

The crude slope is 0.90 (0.52 to 1.29). In the adjusted model the wealth row gives 0.62 kg per unit, t = 3.92 on 233 df (237 children − 3 predictors − 1), p < 0.001. sexF is girls compared with boys. The last three results are the J090 checks described under Diagnostics.

blocks.label: Output.
blocks.html:
Predictor Coefficient 95% CI p-value
Wealth index (per unit) 0.62 0.31 to 0.93 <0.001
Age (per month) 0.18 0.15 to 0.21 <0.001
Sex: girl (vs boy) −0.25 −0.58 to 0.08 0.14

Adjusted R² = 0.41; residual SD 1.28 kg; n = 237.

Interpretation. Adjusting for age and sex, each one-unit higher wealth index is associated with 0.62 kg higher weight on average (95% CI 0.31 to 0.93 kg). Girls weighed 0.25 kg less than boys of the same age and wealth, but the interval (−0.58 to 0.08 kg) is compatible with anything from a moderate deficit to a small excess, so this study cannot tell whether sex matters. The model accounts for about 41% of the variation in weight, leaving room for factors not measured here (illness, feeding, birth weight).

Why did the wealth coefficient fall from 0.90 to 0.62? In a model with wealth and age only (sex barely matters here), least squares gives an exact identity: crude slope = adjusted slope + (age coefficient) × (slope of age on wealth). Here 0.621 + 0.180 × 1.569 = 0.903. Wealthier households’ children were on average 1.57 months older per wealth unit, and each month adds 0.18 kg, so about 0.28 kg of the crude 0.90 was age. Age also did its precision job: without it the residual SD would be 1.59 kg instead of 1.28, and the SE of the wealth coefficient 0.194 instead of 0.158.

What the result does not mean. It does not show that raising a household’s wealth would cause a 0.62 kg gain. The study is cross-sectional and observational, and the wealth index stands for a bundle of things (diet, housing, care-seeking) not measured separately; unmeasured confounding by factors such as parental education or dietary diversity cannot be ruled out, and the wealth index itself may leave residual confounding (recall §11.6). Nor does p = 0.14 show that sex is unrelated to weight. And an average association says nothing certain about any one child.

Reporting. “In a multiple linear regression of weight (kg) on household wealth index, adjusting for age and sex (n = 237 complete cases), wealth was positively associated with weight (adjusted β = 0.62 kg per unit, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.93, p < 0.001; crude β = 0.90). The association between sex and weight was imprecisely estimated (girls −0.25 kg, 95% CI −0.58 to 0.08). Adjusted R² = 0.41. Given the cross-sectional design, the association should not be interpreted causally.”

points.html: Order of reasoning: question and outcome; predictors, each with its reason (exposure, confounder, precision covariate); data preparation and crude analysis; adjusted model; assumptions and diagnostics; interpretation; limits.

A confounder must be associated with the exposure and affect the outcome, off the causal path. A precision covariate affects the outcome but is unrelated to the exposure: it shrinks the SE without shifting the coefficient. Age here was both; sex was only the second.
A crude-to-adjusted shift (0.90 → 0.62) is consistent with confounding and, in linear regression, can be traced exactly. It supports but does not replace the prior reasoning for adjusting.
Every number in the output table earns a plain-language sentence, and the “what this does not mean” step keeps association and causation apart.

questions.prompt: In a two-predictor model, the adjusted coefficient for maternal education (years) on birthweight is 25 g per year, the coefficient for maternal height is 12 g per cm, and the slope of maternal height on education is 0.5 cm per year. What was the crude coefficient for education?
questions.answer: Crude slope = adjusted slope + (height coefficient) × (slope of height on education) = 25 + 12 × 0.5 = 25 + 6 = 31 g per year. About 6 g of the crude 31 g per year reflected the taller stature of more-educated mothers.

questions.prompt: A colleague says “age is a confounder in every child-growth study”. Using the confounder and precision-covariate definitions, explain when age confounds a wealth–weight association and when it is only a precision covariate.
questions.answer: Age affects weight in every such study, and wealth cannot cause a child’s age, so age is never a mediator. But it confounds the wealth–weight association only if it is also associated with wealth in the population studied, for example if wealthier families bring older children to the clinic. Then the crude comparison mixes the wealth difference with an age difference, and adjustment moves the coefficient (as in §12.6: 0.90 → 0.62, with r = 0.16 between age and wealth). If age is unrelated to wealth (say, a sample with the same age distribution in every wealth group), it is only a precision covariate: adjusting leaves the wealth coefficient unchanged but shrinks its SE, because it removes age-driven variation from the residuals. Including it is worthwhile in both cases, but for different reasons.
